strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important gap: conformal prediction for extremely long-tailed multi-class problems where marginal coverage alone can hide severe failures on rare classes.

The prevalence-adjusted softmax (PAS) score is simple, well motivated, and backed by a clean oracle optimality argument for macro-coverage versus expected set size. This is an elegant contribution that practitioners could adopt easily.

The FUZZY CP framework usefully connects standard and classwise conformal prediction through label-weighted quantiles, and the reconformalization step restores marginal coverage for the main FUZZY method.

Experiments are conducted on realistic large-class long-tailed datasets, Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist, with several relevant baselines including standard, classwise, exact classwise, and clustered CP.
The paper is clearly written, with good intuition for why rare classes are harmed by standard CP and why classwise CP can become impractically large in the long-tailed regime.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than major. PAS is essentially a class-prior-adjusted likelihood-ratio score, and FUZZY CP is a fairly natural interpolation/smoothing of classwise conformal thresholds; the paper's strength is in packaging and empirical validation more than in a fundamentally new technical idea.

The strongest theoretical result is oracle-level and does not imply finite-sample macro-coverage or class-conditional guarantees for PAS. In practice PAS still only has marginal coverage, so some claims about improving class-conditional behavior rely heavily on empirical evidence.

The FUZZY method depends on an ad hoc prevalence-based class embedding and bandwidth tuning. The paper explores alternatives in the appendix, but there is no principled selection rule for the mapping, and it is unclear how robust this is beyond the two studied domains.

The empirical evaluation is limited to two image datasets and one base model family. More evidence across architectures, calibration quality levels, non-vision long-tailed tasks, and different score functions would make the claimed generality more convincing.

The experimental protocol has some weaknesses: the paper notes that the validation set is used both for model selection and conformal calibration, which violates the clean exchangeability assumptions, and dismisses this mostly empirically. This is a real concern for a paper centered on coverage guarantees.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the line 'Code for reproducing our experiments is available at' appears without an actual URL, and many implementation choices such as tuning criteria and data splitting details are important for reproducing the tradeoff curves.

The main plots are dense and hard to interpret quantitatively; they show favorable Pareto trends but do not provide uncertainty intervals or statistical tests for the reported improvements in class-conditional metrics.

strengths: The paper targets an important and realistic problem: conformal prediction under extreme long-tailed multiclass distributions, where marginal coverage is insufficient and classwise CP can produce unusably large sets.
The PAS score is simple, intuitive, and supported by a clean oracle argument showing why thresholding p(y|x)/p(y) is appropriate for optimizing macro-coverage versus expected set size.
The paper evaluates on relevant large-scale fine-grained datasets, including Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist, and considers several coverage and set-size metrics rather than only marginal coverage.
The proposed methods are conceptually easy to implement, and the discussion of weighted macro-coverage for endangered or at-risk species is practically motivated.
weaknesses: A central validity issue is that the validation set is used both for model selection and conformal calibration. The paper explicitly acknowledges that this violates exchangeability, but then relies on a weak empirical check for one threshold value. This undermines the stated conformal guarantees in the actual experimental protocol.

Reproducibility is poor: the main text says code is available but the link is blank, and the experimental details are not sufficient to reproduce the figures reliably, especially the splits, tuning choices, and implementation of baselines.

The empirical evidence is narrower than the claims. Results are mostly on two related biodiversity image datasets, with truncated variants derived from them. This makes it hard to know whether the methods generalize beyond this domain or beyond prevalence-correlated classifier errors.

The figures are crowded and mostly qualitative; the paper does not provide enough numerical tables, uncertainty estimates, or statistical variability over seeds/splits. It is difficult to assess the magnitude and robustness of the claimed Pareto improvements.

The comparison protocol is not fully convincing. Hyperparameters for FUZZY and INTERP-Q are swept to show trade-off curves, but the paper does not give a rigorous deployment-time selection rule that preserves the intended guarantees and avoids optimistic test-set interpretation.

Some proposed components are weakly motivated. The prevalence-based class embedding for FUZZY is heuristic, dataset-dependent, and partially duplicates the intuition already captured by PAS; its added value over simpler prevalence reweighting is not clearly established.

INTERP-Q is presented despite lacking a coverage guarantee, and its strong empirical performance further raises the question of whether the more principled FUZZY method is necessary or whether the contribution is mainly heuristic threshold smoothing.

The simulated human-decision experiment is too stylized to support strong claims about downstream utility. Expert verifier/random guesser mixtures are useful sanity checks, but they are not a substitute for user studies or more realistic models of cognitive effort and label verification.

The paper’s main theoretical results are largely oracle or structural results; the practical methods depend heavily on estimated probabilities and class prevalences, but the paper gives limited analysis of sensitivity to calibration error, label noise, or distribution shift.

Overall, the work is coherent and potentially useful, but the evaluation and reproducibility gaps, plus the calibration-protocol validity issue, keep it slightly below the acceptance threshold for a top-tier AI venue.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: conformal prediction for many-class long-tailed classification, where marginal coverage can mask very poor rare-class coverage and classwise CP can yield unusably large sets.

The PAS score is simple, well motivated, and backed by a clean oracle optimality result for macro-coverage/size tradeoffs. The weighted macro-coverage extension is also natural and practically relevant.

The FUZZY CP construction gives a useful interpolation between standard and classwise CP, with a reconformalization step that restores marginal coverage. The paper clearly separates guaranteed and non-guaranteed variants.

Experiments are run on two realistic long-tailed fine-grained image datasets with thousands of classes, multiple target coverage levels, several baselines, and several metrics that expose class-conditional behavior beyond marginal coverage.

The results consistently support the main qualitative claim: the proposed methods improve macro/class-conditional coverage at much smaller set sizes than classwise CP, while retaining marginal coverage for the main guaranteed methods.

The paper is clearly written, with good motivation from plant identification and biodiversity monitoring, and includes useful appendices with proofs, additional mappings, PAS combinations, and a case study.
weaknesses: A central experimental detail weakens the validity story: the validation set is used both for model selection and conformal calibration, which violates the exchangeability assumptions behind the stated conformal guarantees. The paper acknowledges this but only gives a limited empirical check for one threshold on one dataset, which is not enough for a guarantee-focused submission.

The code availability line appears incomplete, which is a reproducibility concern, especially given the many implementation choices in dataset resplitting, model training, calibration, and hyperparameter sweeps.

The empirical scope is still somewhat narrow: all main experiments are image classification with ResNet-50 on two biodiversity-style datasets. It is unclear how well the methods transfer to other long-tailed domains, stronger modern backbones, or classifiers trained with long-tail-specific losses.

Some important baselines and score functions are not fully explored. The paper discusses rank-calibrated class-conditional CP and APS/RAPS-style scores but does not include them as main empirical comparisons, relying instead on an argument that they are less relevant or larger-set methods.

The tuning of FUZZY bandwidths and INTERP-Q weights is only lightly addressed. The paper says practitioners can tune to a desired average set size using calibration data, but a principled selection protocol and its effect on validity/utility are not evaluated in depth.

Several key empirical claims are supported primarily by dense plots rather than tables or confidence intervals. This makes it hard to assess statistical variability, especially for rare-class metrics and truncated dataset estimates of marginal quantities.

The novelty is solid but not overwhelming: PAS is an elegant reweighting of softmax by prevalence and FUZZY is a natural label-weighted conformal interpolation. The contribution is valuable, but the core ideas are relatively simple extensions of existing conformal machinery.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant gap: conformal prediction for many-class long-tailed classification, where marginal coverage can hide severe failures on rare classes and classwise CP produces unusably large sets.

The prevalence-adjusted softmax score is simple, intuitive, and theoretically motivated by an oracle optimality result for macro-coverage/expected-size trade-offs. This makes the method easy to implement while connecting it to a clear population objective.

The empirical results on Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist-2018 are convincing in showing a useful middle ground: PAS and INTERP-Q substantially improve macro/class-conditional coverage metrics over standard CP while keeping set sizes far below classwise CP.

The paper is well written and generally clear. The distinction between marginal coverage, macro-coverage, and class-conditional coverage is useful, and the evaluation metrics directly reflect the intended long-tailed use case.
The appendices provide nontrivial additional material, including proofs, focal-loss experiments, truncated-dataset evaluations, additional fuzzy variants, and a plant-conservation case study.
weaknesses: The main guarantees remain marginal coverage only for PAS, not macro-coverage or class-conditional coverage. The improved macro/class-conditional behavior is empirical and depends on the classifier/prior estimates, so some claims about targeting macro-coverage should be phrased more cautiously.

INTERP-Q has only a weak 1-2alpha marginal coverage guarantee, and the paper relies on empirical coverage near 1-alpha. For alpha=0.1 this formal guarantee is only 80%, which is substantially below the target and limits the method's theoretical appeal.

The interpolation parameter tau is swept to trace trade-off curves, but the paper does not provide a statistically valid or practically complete model-selection protocol for choosing tau while preserving coverage. The discussion acknowledges this but leaves an important deployment question unresolved.

Novelty is moderate rather than high. PAS resembles prior/logit adjustment or likelihood-ratio style reweighting for long-tailed/balanced classification, and the paper could position this connection more deeply and compare to more prior-adjusted conformal scores.

The experimental scope is somewhat narrow: two fine-grained image datasets, one main architecture, and limited comparison to adaptive conformal methods or long-tail learning/calibration baselines. The dismissal of APS/RAPS as larger-set methods is plausible but would be stronger with direct empirical comparison.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript as presented: the code availability line appears blank, and important implementation details such as exact hyperparameter selection, random seeds, and computational cost of large-class set construction are not fully specified.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: conformal prediction for long-tailed, many-class classification, where standard marginal coverage can badly neglect rare classes and classwise conformal sets can become unusably large.
The prevalence-adjusted softmax idea is simple, easy to implement, and supported by a clean oracle motivation for optimizing macro-coverage rather than marginal coverage.

The empirical results on Pl@ntNet-300K show a meaningful trade-off improvement over standard conformal prediction: e.g., at 90% marginal coverage, PAS substantially reduces the fraction of very poorly covered classes with only a modest increase in average set size.
The paper is generally clearly written and includes useful appendices with proofs, dataset split details, and additional analyses such as focal loss and endangered-species weighting.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. PAS is essentially a prior/prevalence-adjusted likelihood-ratio score, closely related in spirit to long-tail logit adjustment, balanced posteriors, and label-shift reweighting. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish the contribution from these nearby ideas beyond conformalizing the score.

The main guarantee for PAS remains only marginal coverage; the desired class-conditional or macro-coverage improvements are empirical and can fail for individual rare classes. The paper itself shows an endangered species with 0 coverage under PAS, which weakens the central motivation.

INTERP-Q has a weak theoretical guarantee of only 1-2α marginal coverage, which is not competitive when users ask for 1-α coverage. The claim that this is conservative is based only on limited empirical evidence.

The evaluation is too narrow for a top-tier acceptance: only two image datasets, one main architecture, limited model/loss variation, no confidence intervals or repeated split analysis, and no strong evidence that the conclusions generalize beyond these datasets.

Several relevant baselines are missing or underdeveloped, including stronger conformal scores such as APS/RAPS-style methods, rank-calibrated class-conditional methods mentioned in the related work, top-k or calibrated top-k baselines, and stronger long-tail classifier adjustments combined with conformal prediction.

The rare-class evaluation is statistically fragile. Full long-tailed test sets have very few examples for many classes, while truncated datasets remove exactly the rarest classes that motivate the work. The paper does not quantify uncertainty in macro-coverage or per-class undercoverage metrics.

Some claims are overstated. The empirical statement that PAS is Pareto optimal is not justified beyond the plotted methods, and the oracle optimality result does not imply optimality when using estimated softmax probabilities and empirical prevalences.
Practical tuning is unresolved. The paper admits that choosing INTERP-Q parameters by calibration-set set size violates exchangeability, but does not provide a principled valid tuning procedure.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the code availability line appears blank, and important details such as seeds, preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, and baseline tuning are insufficient for confident reproduction.
Overall, the paper is coherent and technically plausible, but the contribution feels incremental and the empirical support is not strong enough for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: conformal prediction for highly long-tailed many-class classification, where marginal coverage can hide severe rare-class undercoverage and classwise CP becomes unusably large.

The main PAS idea is simple, well-motivated, and theoretically grounded through an oracle optimality result for macro-coverage/expected-size tradeoffs. The weighted extension is also natural and practically useful for prioritizing endangered or otherwise important classes.
INTERP-Q is a pragmatic and easy-to-implement procedure that exposes a useful knob between standard and classwise behavior; despite its simplicity, the empirical tradeoff curves are compelling.

The evaluation is strong for the paper’s target setting: two large long-tailed fine-grained datasets, thousands of classes, comparison to standard, classwise, and clustered CP baselines, multiple miscoverage levels, and several metrics capturing both marginal and class-conditional behavior.

The empirical results show clear practical gains: PAS and INTERP-Q substantially improve macro/class-conditional coverage with modest set-size increases, while classwise CP yields prohibitively large sets.
The paper is clearly written, with good positioning, useful appendices, proof details, extra truncated-dataset evaluation, focal-loss experiments, and a domain-motivated Pl@ntNet case study.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee for INTERP-Q is only marginal coverage at least 1-2α, which is substantially weaker than the desired 1-α guarantee and somewhat mismatched with the empirical presentation emphasizing near-1-α behavior.

PAS has only standard marginal conformal validity; its macro-coverage benefits rely on model quality and prevalence estimates. The paper could better characterize when prevalence adjustment helps or hurts, especially under label-distribution estimation error or calibration/test label shift.

The evaluation, while strong, is concentrated on image classification with a ResNet-50 backbone and two biodiversity-style datasets. Additional domains or modern stronger long-tail classifiers would improve confidence in generality.

The choice of INTERP-Q parameter τ is not fully resolved. The discussion suggests choosing τ by calibration-set average size despite an exchangeability violation; this practical selection issue deserves a more principled treatment or validation procedure.

Baselines could be broader: comparisons to top-k/risk-controlling set predictors, long-tail calibration/logit-adjusted models, or alternative conformal scores beyond softmax/PAS would clarify whether gains come from the proposed procedures specifically or from prevalence-aware scoring more generally.
Reproducibility is mostly good in terms of dataset/model details, but the manuscript text appears to say code is available without a visible URL, which should be fixed before publication.
